title: Sh-M
hook: shem, a name, gives Exodus its Hebrew title, Shemot

segments.voice: Yesterday, N-S-A: nasa, to lift and to carry, the root behind Naso. Your line was lift. What did you pick up for someone, even something small? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

Roll call, first morning of school. The teacher reads down the list, reaches a name she has never seen, pauses, and takes a guess. The whole room turns to look at the kid whose name it is. Will they correct her, or let it slide for the rest of the year? The second book of the Torah opens with a roll call of its own: "Now these are the names of the children of Israel, which came into Egypt; every man and his household came with Jacob." Then the sons of Jacob are listed, one by one. The book is about to tell how a family was put to hard labor under taskmasters. Before any of that, it says their names. Today's root is the word it starts with.
screen: `A TEACHER GUESSES AT A NAME.` → `EXODUS OPENS WITH A ROLL CALL.` → `NAMES BEFORE SLAVERY.`

segments.voice: Sh-M. Two letters, shin and mem. Shem: a name. In Hebrew the second book takes its title from that opening verse: Shemot, names. English calls it Exodus, the way out. Hebrew calls it the names. Turn the word a few ways. First, the roll call. Genesis has already listed these same sons going down to Egypt. So why list them again? The medieval commentator Rashi answers that they are counted again to show how dear they are, the way God brings out the stars by number and calls each one by name. A midrash adds a teaching about Egypt itself: the people were redeemed, in part, because they did not change their names. Far from home, under hard masters, they kept being who they had been called. Second, a name for God that works by not being a name. At the burning bush, Moses asks what name he should give the people, and the answer is "I AM THAT I AM." Today, in everyday speech, some Jews refer to God simply as Hashem: the Name. It is a way of speaking of God with care, without saying the holy name lightly. Third, a name you build. Ecclesiastes says, "A good name is better than precious ointment." The Hebrew is a pun: tov shem mi-shemen tov, a good shem over good shemen, oil. Perfume fades by evening. The name you earn stays in the room after you leave. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. To say someone's name properly is to tell them they are a person, not a number on a list. That is what the first verse of Shemot does for a family about to be worked as labor. Names matter.
screen: `SHEMOT: THE BOOK OF NAMES.` · `COUNTED AGAIN, LIKE THE STARS.` · `HASHEM: THE NAME.` · `A GOOD NAME OVER GOOD OIL.` · then, large: `NAMES MATTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn someone's name properly. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one person whose name you've been saying a little wrong, or never quite caught: a coworker, a neighbor, the person who hands you your coffee. Say it silently, the way you've been saying it. Then plan the question, something simple: I want to get your name right, how do you say it? If there's someone whose name you never learned at all, they are the one. For the rest of the sit, let the names of people you love pass through your mind, one at a time, slowly, the way the book of names begins. If you pray, you can hold each one before God as it comes. The bell holds the time.
screen: `ONE NAME YOU'VE BEEN GETTING WRONG.` · `PLAN THE QUESTION.` · `NAMES YOU LOVE, ONE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Sh-M. Shin, mem: shem, a name. Shemot, the names, the Hebrew title of Exodus. Hashem, the Name. Today's word.
Your line: names matter. Today, ask one person how to say their name, and then use it, properly, at least once before the day ends. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

notes: Rashi on Exodus 1:1 paraphrased: though Scripture counted them in their lifetime (Genesis 46), it counts them again at their death to show how dear they are, likened to the stars brought out and brought in by number and name (Isaiah 40:26). Confirm the paraphrase.

The midrash that Israel was redeemed from Egypt because they did not change their names (with language, etc.) is cited as Vayikra Rabbah 32:5; parallels exist (e.g. Mekhilta, Shir HaShirim Rabbah). Confirm the reference.
Rashi is introduced as a medieval commentator.
Hashem: described as a usage 'some Jews' keep in everyday speech, to avoid saying the divine name lightly. Confirm framing.
Ecclesiastes 7:1 Hebrew 'tov shem mi-shemen tov'; the script gives it as 'tov shem mi-shemen'. Confirm transliteration.
howItsDone paraphrases Pirkei Avot 4:13 (4:17 in some numberings): three crowns, and the crown of a good name rises above them. Confirm numbering.
